overall.pooledNote: Pooled over five different starting conditions: a mixture, not an estimate for any single rule set.

heterogeneity.note: Seeded permutation test (chi-square statistic) of first-mover wins across the five conditions, decisive games only. Exploratory: five conditions screened at once, no correction for multiple looks.

B.note: plus = games where the first mover won in B but not in A (same seed and first mover); minus = the reverse

C.note: plus = games where the first mover won in C but not in A (same seed and first mover); minus = the reverse

D.note: plus = games where the first mover won in D but not in A (same seed and first mover); minus = the reverse

perCondition.note: With 20 decisive games a first-mover share must reach at least this many wins (75%) before an exact test rejects a 50/50 split at 5%, and a 95% interval is roughly +/- 20 points wide. Smaller real advantages are invisible at this sample size.

findings.text: A (3/3): first mover won 33/59 (56%, 95% CI 43%–68%, exact p vs 50% = 0.435). The interval includes 50%: no reliable first-mover effect at n = 60. Mean length 13.617 turns (95% CI 10.983–16.251), turn-limit rate 3%.

B (3/3): first mover won 36/60 (60%, 95% CI 47%–71%, exact p vs 50% = 0.155). The interval includes 50%: no reliable first-mover effect at n = 60. Mean length 16.533 turns (95% CI 12.458–20.609), turn-limit rate 10%.

C (2/3): first mover won 37/60 (62%, 95% CI 49%–73%, exact p vs 50% = 0.092). The interval includes 50%: no reliable first-mover effect at n = 60. Mean length 14.617 turns (95% CI 11.153–18.08), turn-limit rate 7%.

C: the side that started with more pieces won 23/60 (38%, 95% CI 27%–51%, exact p vs 50% = 0.092). More pieces also means more actions per turn and a larger victory requirement, so this is the effect of the whole package, not of piece count alone.

D (2/3): first mover won 37/60 (62%, 95% CI 49%–73%, exact p vs 50% = 0.092). The interval includes 50%: no reliable first-mover effect at n = 60. Mean length 14.967 turns (95% CI 11.21–18.723), turn-limit rate 8%.

D: the side that started with more pieces won 23/60 (38%, 95% CI 27%–51%, exact p vs 50% = 0.092). More pieces also means more actions per turn and a larger victory requirement, so this is the effect of the whole package, not of piece count alone.
All 240 games pooled: first mover won 143/239 (60%, 95% CI 54%–66%, exact p vs 50% = 0.003). Pooled across different rules, so it only says whether a first-mover tendency shows up broadly.

Do the five conditions differ in first-mover win rate? Permutation test p = 0.915. No evidence that starting piece count changes first-mover advantage at this sample size. This is absence of evidence, not evidence of no effect.

B vs A on the same seed and first mover: first-mover outcome flipped toward the first mover in 15 pairs and away in 12 (exact sign test p = 0.701). RNG trajectories: 0/60 games never diverged from the reference RNG sequence, so pairs share a seed but not a game.

C vs A on the same seed and first mover: first-mover outcome flipped toward the first mover in 16 pairs and away in 12 (exact sign test p = 0.572). RNG trajectories: 0/60 games never diverged from the reference RNG sequence, so pairs share a seed but not a game.

D vs A on the same seed and first mover: first-mover outcome flipped toward the first mover in 15 pairs and away in 11 (exact sign test p = 0.557). RNG trajectories: 0/60 games never diverged from the reference RNG sequence, so pairs share a seed but not a game.
Game length (mean turns): A 13.617, B 16.533, C 14.617, D 14.967. Fewer pieces means fewer actions per turn but also fewer pieces to bring across.

Conveyor-belt moves (a piece stepping on its own side's trap and being carried forward): A 16/game (more-conveyor side won 36/58); B 14.817/game (more-conveyor side won 34/56); C 13.833/game (more-conveyor side won 32/57); D 14.317/game (more-conveyor side won 38/57). An association with winning is not proof that conveyors cause wins: stronger positions also create more chances to use them.
Both sides use the same deterministic planner and weights, so "Human side" and "AI side" are board directions, not different players. Results describe this planner playing itself, not human play.
These 100 games are exploratory. They were looked at to form hypotheses and cannot also serve as the holdout that tests them.
